By parsing the query image into discrete building `thing' instances and continuous `stuff' regions comprising road, vegetation, and water, we establish a holistic alignment with this map to robustly optimize the camera pose. To enable reliable panoptic perception, we develop a new automated pipeline that constructs AirPan - the largest aerial panoptic segmentation dataset to date, comprising 85k images with pixel-accurate annotations. This empowers our panoptic segmentation model to exhibit remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LoD-Loc v4 consistently outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines by a significant margin. Most notably, it successfully maintains reliable localization in building-less scenarios, completely overcoming the catastrophic failures of prior building-centric paradigms.

title: PeptSol: A Translational Benchmark for Protected-Peptide Solubility in Drug Manufacturing
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 19 tables. Accepted at the AI for Drug Discovery workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Liquid-phase peptide synthesis (LPPS) offers a scalable route to peptide manufacturing, but route development still depends on empirical solvent screens because each protected intermediate must be soluble for reaction and recoverable for purification. The protecting groups, terminal modifications, and noncanonical residues that govern this behaviour are poorly represented in existing peptide property benchmarks, limiting the ability to develop and rigorously evaluate molecular representation models for LPPS-relevant prediction tasks. We introduce PeptSol, an open benchmark of 1388 hand-curated protected-peptide solubility measurements with chemistry-aware splits. The measurements span only 84 parent sequences and 101 protected structures, and 92.5% come from a single historical programme. Across seven frozen molecular encoders, the best macro-F1 is 0.843 on binary solubility for the historical subset under a peptide-held-out split; the harder three-class ordinal task reaches 0.614 in that cell. No foundation model consistently outperforms a baseline combining chemical fingerprints with explicit molecular descriptors, and model rankings vary across prediction tasks and data splits. The dataset, evaluation protocol, and baselines establish a standard for measuring progress on molecular representations for synthesis-aware peptide developability.

title: DuSE-Bench: Benchmarking Joint Reasoning over Evolving Dialogue and Documents
summary: Persistent Web information assistants must combine evolving document facts with user requirements established and revised across sessions. Yet systematic evaluation of how changes in both sources affect response requirements and evidence attribution remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce Dual-Source Evolution Benchmark (DuSE-Bench), a benchmark comprising 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 whose required premises originate in both dialogue and documents. An evolving Support Graph guides task construction and preserves links from updated facts and reused conclusions to original turns and passages. Task annotations distinguish grounding source from state dependence and enable separate evaluation of response content, response type, and source attribution. Experiments across 11 baseline configurations reveal persistent challenges in joint reasoning over evolving dialogue and documents, with content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaching at most 56.7%. Moreover, improvements in content accuracy can coincide with poorer response choice, while content-correct responses frequently lack complete attribution to original evidence. Matched evidence substitutions further show that the effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other. These findings motivate coordinating dialogue memory and document retrieval to apply current user requirements and document facts together while preserving their original support. The data are available at https://github.com/JianfengGao7/DuSE-Bench.

title: Designing Informative Actions: Action Construction for Long-Horizon Research Agents
summary: Large language model agents support automated scientific research by connecting literature analysis and planning with experimentation. Evaluating which action an agent selects does not establish which experiment its instruction specifies, because omitted interventions or replication counts leave consequential choices to the executor. We introduce a reading-set framework for evaluating action construction under a common cost rule. Across 30 synthetic states, complete-design requests increase affordable efficiency by 465.98% and 327.91% relative to the action-name baseline in the two model families, respectively. An author-constructed research-action evaluation dataset provides 60 scenarios for complementary judgment evaluation. On this dataset, the scenario-level information-per-cost measure has a mean within-scenario correlation of 0.733 with judgments from 18 human participants. The framework makes design specification and execution ambiguity measurable, providing a reproducible basis for assessing how research agents translate scientific intent into informative, budget-feasible experiments.

title: Decision-Centric Research: A Calibrated Decision Model and Benchmark for Scientific Agents
summary: Scientific agents make consequential choices about evidence, next actions and research strategy, but choices embedded in generated text are difficult to evaluate independently. Decision-Centric Research (DCR) is introduced to make individual choices the common unit of supervision, prediction and evaluation through typed predictions over an explicit Research State. DCR defines 24 decision types, ten of which are instantiated in the Research Decision Benchmark (RD-Bench) of 2,000 rule-generated cases. The Decision-Centric Research Model (DCRM) shares a candidate-token readout across types to produce answers and option probabilities in one forward pass. Under a held-out research-domain split, a 0.6B DCRM (state-aware) achieves 89.4% Top-1 accuracy, compared with 27.8% for DCRM (question-only) trained with the same recipe and 36.4% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. All 30 type-seed comparisons against DCRM (question-only) are significant after Holm correction. After held-out calibration, the resulting prediction sets contain a mean of 1.515 candidates at 97.1% empirical label coverage, reducing mean set size by 57.4% relative to DCRM (question-only) at similar coverage. These results establish a compact state-aware decision layer with accurate typed prediction and an inspectable uncertainty interface.

title: One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $λ$. The sign of $λ$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($λ{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($λ{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $λ{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.

title: Crop Mapping Evaluation under Sampling Bias
summary: Government agencies use crop maps to estimate production, monitor food security, and set agricultural policy. These crop maps are usually validated against field labels, but these labels are rarely a random sample of the area the map covers. Field teams tend to label parcels near roads and skip ones that are small or hard to reach, so performance measured on held-out labels mainly describes the places they visited. We call the difference between this reported performance and performance over the whole mapped region the deployment performance gap. To estimate performance over the whole region, we use a weighted form of prediction-powered inference (PPI). The classifier's predictions on unlabeled points across the region give a first estimate, and its errors on the labeled points correct that estimate, with more weight on labels from under-sampled conditions. We test this in five European regions where crop registers label every declared parcel, so the true performance is known. Simulating six documented collection practices there produces gaps of up to 0.20 macro-F1. On the collection rule that creates the largest gap in each region, 5 km block cross-validation still overestimates macro-F1 by as much as 0.18, while PPI with weights estimated from satellite embeddings reduces the largest error across regions to 0.07. Importance-weighted cross-validation with the same weights does almost as well, so most of the improvement comes from the weights themselves. We also apply the method to three Kenyan datasets that have no region-wide reference labels. For a roadside dataset collected with helmet-mounted cameras, the estimated macro-F1 falls from 0.93 under random cross-validation to 0.61, although the correction relies on a small number of heavily weighted labels. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/pappi.

title: BridgeDock: Taming Generative Co-Folding Prior for Molecular Docking with Diffusion Bridge
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 29 pages, 4 figures, including appendices
summary: Molecular docking aims to predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex; in the conventional structure-based setting, it is conditioned on an input protein structure and ligand, often starting from an apo receptor in flexible docking or a holo receptor in rigid docking. Recent co-folding models exemplified by AlphaFold 3 achieve strong accuracy in protein-ligand complex prediction, but they typically generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and therefore do not directly use apo structures as structural priors in docking, leading to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings. We present BridgeDock, a framework that adapts pretrained co-folding backbones to flexible docking by modeling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, allowing generation from the initial protein-ligand state rather than from Gaussian noise. To make this bridge formulation compatible with pretrained denoisers, we introduce an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model. Experiments on standard flexible docking benchmarks show that BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines. Moreover, BridgeDock is computationally efficient at inference time and remains effective even with very few denoising steps.

title: Streaming Virtual Metrology via Lightweight Adaptation under Temporal Distribution Shifts
summary: Virtual metrology (VM) aims to estimate costly or delayed metrology variables from heterogeneous sensor signals and in-line measurements, and it acts as a critical component of semiconductor manufacturing. While recent data-driven models have improved VM accuracy, most are trained in batch settings and assume stationary data distributions. In practice, however, production environments evolve continuously due to equipment degradation, process adjustments, and maintenance events, making conventional batch-trained VM models difficult to maintain under temporal distribution shifts. In this work, we propose GRAPE (Global Regression with Adaptive Prediction Enhancement), a practical online learning framework for VM in evolving wafer-processing environments. GRAPE integrates a stable global predictor based on interpretable representations with two lightweight streaming adapters that correct feature-level and environment-level shifts through online updates. Experiments on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets, including chronologically held-out blind-test streams, show that GRAPE improves robustness and generalization under real temporal drift compared with both conventional batch-learning methods and existing online learning baselines.

title: VCoT-SQL: Enhancing Text-to-SQL Generation through Dual Chain-of-Thought Validation Training
summary: Open-source LLMs provide a flexible alternative to closed-source models for Text-to-SQL but still struggle with complex queries. Finetuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) data improves reasoning, yet standard datasets lack CoT annotations, requiring synthetic generation. Existing synthesis methods only verify the final answer, allowing flawed reasoning steps to corrupt the training data. We propose VCoT-SQL, a framework that improves Text-to-SQL generation through intermediate-step validated CoT supervision and a dedicated SQL validator, which enables small open-source models to outperform frontier closed-source models. VCoT-SQL trains two complementary models on curated reasoning traces: an SQL generator using clause-level CoT templates where reasoning steps are verified via execution and schema alignment checks, and an SQL validator using diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic, and type level errors. We further design a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline that integrates and refines complementary retrieval strategies to distill relevant database elements. VCoT-SQL achieves 66.82% execution accuracy on challenging dataset BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD. Notably, our CoT synthesis relies on 7B models yet outperforms methods that use 72B-scale or even proprietary closed source teachers for data generation, demonstrating that rigorous step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up teacher model size. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/INTREBID/VCoT-SQL.

title: AdKnob: Ad Intensity Control and Labeling for LLM-Native Advertising
summary: Large language model (LLM)-native advertising has emerged as a viable monetization channel as LLM service providers seek sustainable revenue streams. However, integrating native ads into LLM responses introduces two largely understudied challenges: (1) controlling ad intensity -- how prominently advertising content appears -- and (2) ad labeling -- identifying which segments of the generated text constitute advertising. We propose AdKnob, a framework jointly addressing both challenges. For ad intensity control, we introduce new ad control tokens without pretrained semantic associations and align the model via direct preference optimization to generate ads at each desired level. For ad labeling, we propose an attention rollout-based attribution mechanism that identifies ad segments by tracing their attribution to input ad-related tokens, requiring no additional inference cost. We further construct MI-KnobSet, the first multi-level ad intensity preference dataset for LLM-native ads. Experiments across six LLMs and human evaluations show that AdKnob achieves uniformly spaced ad intensities where baselines collapse to a narrow range, achieves the highest ad labeling accuracy while being over 500x faster than the strongest baseline, and is preferred over baselines by human evaluators up to 89.6% of the time.

title: Adaptive-Policy Distillation: Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), which uses reverse-KL supervision on student rollouts to transfer a context-conditioned model's behavior into student model parameters for closed-book inference, has shown strong results. However, we find that this success does not translate to knowledge injection: across two document-QA benchmarks, OPD injects document knowledge far less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation. We trace this reversal to two failures that are structural, yet sparse across token positions. Reverse KL weights its gradient by the student distribution and therefore barely lifts document-specific tokens the student considers unlikely; after forward KL restores this signal, student rollouts expose later positions on the target trajectory only after generating the preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length. Motivated by the concentration of teacher-student divergence at these hard positions, we propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose per-token gate jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, withdrawing both interventions as the student learns. Without labels or a verifier, APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6%, achieving the best scores of 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 MRR on BioASQ.

title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
summary: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.

title: Benchmarking Machine-Learning Classifiers for Neoantigen Immunogenicity Prediction and the Limits of SHAP Interpretability
summary:
Personalized cancer vaccines require prioritizing, among hundreds of candidate mutant peptides, the few that will induce a T-cell response. This study asks what general-purpose machine learning achieves on that task, and whether the features such models identify as important can be trusted.
  We make three contributions. The first is a benchmark of sixty models: twelve supervised classifier families, each in five configurations, evaluated on the Immunogenic Tumor Specific Neoantigen database (ITSNdb; 199 experimentally validated neoantigens, 129 immunogenic and 70 non-immunogenic). All sixty are compared under one stratified k-fold cross-validation protocol, in which the data used to choose a configuration are never the data used to score it. The second is an interpretability study that combines SHAP with feature ablation. The third is a shuffled-label control that tests whether a SHAP value has been earned.
  Two results follow, and both run against current practice. First, the classical linear models lead the ranking. The gradient-boosted ensembles and neural networks that dominate recent work bring no advantage. Second, SHAP can fail on high-cardinality categorical features. Ablation establishes the presenting HLA allele as the dominant input and the source gene as dispensable. SHAP reports the opposite, assigning 68.7% to 81.7% of its total value to the source gene in every model that gives each gene its own weight. Shuffling the gene labels at random among the peptides resolves the contradiction: the meaningless column earns the same SHAP value as the real one. That value measures only that ITSNdb contains 173 genes for 199 peptides. We therefore recommend that SHAP values for high-cardinality categorical annotations in cohorts of this size always be reported against such a shuffled-label control, and we describe one in full.

title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Code at https://github.com/dengzhe-hou/S1CogBench
summary: Language models are no longer used only to generate text. Software also asks them for decisions, in routing, guardrails, and automated gates. System One decision models, also called typed decision models, such as Jev and Laya, return one fast decision over the legal options, leaving no text to inspect. However, a fast, well-formed decision does not show that the model used the evidence. Cognitive experiments can test this, because they vary task demands and measure how behavior changes, yet existing cognitive benchmarks evaluate language and multimodal models. We introduce S1CogBench to ask what these models can and cannot do on 24 cognitive tasks, evaluating five open models and Jev and keeping conditions and scoring apart from disclosed adaptations. We find that decision models vary widely in reliability, acting well does not imply predicting humans, aggregate scores hide how decisions respond to conditions, and speed comes mainly from answering without generation. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments, and it gives a shared test of whether their decisions respond to evidence, feedback, memory load, and future opportunities before software relies on them.

title: Benchmarking Classical Machine Learning Models for Shading-Fault Detection in Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems Using Real Sensor Data
summary: Most published comparisons of machine-learning classifiers for photovoltaic (PV) fault detection are validated on simulated faults. We compare seven classical and ensemble-tree classifiers on the Réunion dataset, a 4 kW domestic rooftop plant on which shading faults were physically staged and logged. Readings within a staged episode are near-duplicates, so every train/test split is grouped by episode. A 20,800-row subsample that retains all 17 fault episodes was evaluated with three repeats of five-fold group-aware nested cross-validation, with synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) applied inside the training folds. Random Forest and XGBoost gave the highest mean accuracy (0.838 and 0.831) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC; 0.526 and 0.522). After Holm correction across the 21 pairwise Wilcoxon tests, only Random Forest's accuracy advantage over k-nearest neighbours and the multi-layer perceptron remained significant. Logistic Regression and the Decision Tree (accuracy 0.820) could be separated neither from the ensembles nor from the weakest models. SMOTE lowered binary MCC for six of the seven classifiers. Errors were concentrated in whole episodes: the Random Forest almost entirely missed four of the 17 fault episodes, including one of two uniform-shading and two of five intermittent-shading episodes. A post-hoc diagnostic shows that the no-fault rows were sampled over a wider range of times of day and output levels than the fault rows. Clock time alone reaches an MCC of 0.44, and PV-side voltage alone 0.72. The reported scores therefore reflect operating-condition differences as well as shading signatures. We release the pipeline and the diagnostics, and identify matched no-fault sampling as the step needed before the classifier ranking can be generalised.

title: What matters in classical machine learning for non-intrusive load monitoring? A factorial benchmark on REFIT with validation on unseen houses
summary: Published classical machine-learning results for appliance ON/OFF classification in nonintrusive load monitoring (NILM) range from F1-type scores of 0.53 to 0.98, and the sources of this spread have not been separated. This study separates them with a factorial benchmark on REFIT: seven models, two feature sets and four class-imbalance strategies for five appliances (270 fitted configurations), each evaluated by pooled nested cross-validation and on houses unseen during training, with robustness checks. An analysis of variance shows that the appliance explains 38% of the variance in F1, the feature set 13% and the model only 8%. Engineered rolling-window features raised the mean F1 score by 52% under both protocols. Other conclusions changed on unseen houses: the support-weighted F1 score of the best pooled configurations fell from 0.548 to 0.447, the differences between the models selected by pooled validation were no longer significant, and the benefit of class weighting over no correction rose from 32% to 69%. In a nested comparison, house-grouped selection on the training houses improved F1 on unseen houses for three of five appliances, by up to 0.110, and was within 0.007 for the other two. These findings held across four house partitions and without the solar-affected houses. A same-protocol convolutional network reached a weighted F1 score of 0.50, about 0.05 above the classical models (0.45) and far below the published deep-learning scores of 0.78 to 0.91, which were obtained under a different protocol. The results support low-cost appliance monitoring in buildings and yield a NILM reporting checklist.

title: UI-UG 2: Advancing Mobile UI Understanding and Generation with Fine-Grained Supervision and Reinforcement Learning
comment: 30 pages, 17 figures, 10 tables, including references and appendices
summary: Mobile UI understanding and generation require both fine-grained component perception and reliable structured synthesis. Inspired by the unified direction introduced by UI-UG, we present UI-UG 2, a compact 4B-parameter multimodal large language model (MLLM) that advances mobile UI Understanding and Generation with broader task coverage, a front-end-aligned taxonomy, and online render-aware reinforcement learning. UI-UG 2 constructs a multi-source understanding corpus from RICO, VINS, Android in the Wild, and Android Control, annotated with an 80-category two-level UI taxonomy aligned with front-end component semantics, and pairs it with over 5,000 requirement-screenshot-JSON tuples for progressive structured UI generation through a domain-specific language (DSL). For understanding, UI-UG 2 introduces decomposed rewards for category prediction, OCR fidelity, color recognition, dense grounding, and GUI grounding. Unlike the offline Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-style generation optimization in UI-UG, UI-UG 2 optimizes generation through end-to-end online Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): sampled DSL outputs are rendered with a Playwright-based server-side pipeline and evaluated using LLM-as-a-Judge and contrastive preference ranking. Experiments show that UI-UG 2 achieves the strongest referring and dense-grounding results among the evaluated models on our 80-category benchmark, and achieves the best composite generation score among compared models at a compact scale (4B). More importantly, we observe a consistent understanding-to-generation transfer: adding fine-grained UI perception supervision improves generation quality under a fixed training budget, suggesting that component-level semantics provide a shared representational foundation for both tasks.

title: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities for cross-lingual transfer of medical knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages to support access to healthcare information. However, medical question-answering (QA) datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs remain scarce for Tetun. To address this gap, we translated MedAlpaca's Medical Flashcards and WikiDoc Patient Information collections into Tetun using Gemini 2.5 Flash, producing 39,077 medical QA pairs. Translation quality was assessed on 50 randomly sampled QA pairs (100 documents) using automatic metrics against human reference translations and evaluations by two native Tetun-speaking healthcare professionals, focusing on medical accuracy and Tetun fluency. Human translations achieved higher mean ratings than LLM-generated translations for both criteria (4.43/5 vs. 4.02/5), with statistically significant differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001). To assess downstream utility, we fine-tuned Gemma and Llama variants on the translated MedAlpaca dataset using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and evaluated them on 325 Tetun-translated United States Medical Licensing Examination multiple-choice questions. Gemma 4 12B fine-tuned using QLoRA achieved relative improvements in mean accuracy of 10.79% with 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) inference and 10.42% after merging the LoRA adapters into the BF16 base model, compared with the corresponding base models. These results highlight the viability of automatic dataset translation for Tetun medical QA and the effectiveness of PEFT in enhancing model performance. The datasets, models, and evaluation resources are accessible at https://github.com/labadain/labadain-medqa to support reproducible research on Tetun medical QA and facilitate machine translation, cross lingual, and multilingual research.

title: MarkovTS: Pretrained State-Transition Representations for Zero-Shot Time Series Generation
summary: Across heterogeneous real-world domains, time-series generation supports simulation, model development, and data augmentation by generating sequences that preserve target-domain statistics and temporal dependencies when real observations are scarce or costly. However, existing methods predominantly address in-domain generation, limiting their reuse in unseen domains. We study reference-conditioned zero-shot time series generation: target domains are unseen during pretraining, generation uses a single target-domain reference sequence, and no model parameters are updated. MarkovTS characterizes sequence evolution through local morphologies and their ordered transitions at multiple temporal scales. Its pretrained encoder quantizes normalized time-series patches into multiscale morphological states with a state codebook, while a transition codebook encodes contextual transitions between adjacent intervals. These transferable state-transition representations condition a pretrained flow-matching model. At generation, the frozen model combines a reference-derived condition with independent Gaussian noise to produce stochastic samples that retain the reference's temporal organization. Across 12 unseen target datasets, MarkovTS outperforms strong baselines in most distributional comparisons and generates diverse, reference-consistent sequences. As downstream augmentation, its samples yield overall gains across forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection benchmarks and diverse model families. Our code is available at https://github.com/blisky-li/MarkovTS.

title: HieraNTP: Structured Risk Representations for Time-Series Anomaly Detection via Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction
summary: Time-series anomaly detection commonly converts deviations from learned temporal regularities into anomaly scores. This practice can conflate violations of temporal regularity with task-specific anomaly judgments: the same deviation may be anomalous under one task definition and benign under another. Aggregating heterogeneous deviations into a single score before task-specific adaptation can obscure the evidence needed to distinguish these cases. We introduce HieraNTP, a Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction framework that separates self-supervised predictive modeling from task-specific risk interpretation. HieraNTP pretrains a hierarchical tokenizer and a causal next-token predictor to capture temporal regularities at multiple scales. It then organizes prediction discrepancies into a structured risk representation, preserving complementary evidence across temporal scales in token, local-statistic, and observation spaces. A task-adaptive detector uses anomaly labels to select and combine this evidence for the target task. Across anomaly detection benchmarks, HieraNTP improves VUS-PR by 12.0% on TSB-AD-U and 15.5% on TSB-AD-M relative to the strongest baselines, and achieves the highest composite score on both TAB tracks, with controlled comparisons supporting the value of retaining distinct evidence. Our code is available at https://github.com/blisky-li/HieraNTP.

title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
summary: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.

title: IJev: Order-Invariant Decisions via Iterated Cyclic Reordering
summary: System One decision models answer a choice question in one forward pass, but their answer depends on the order in which options are listed, and their probabilities carry a prior over answer labels. An invariant ordering operator is any fixed function that returns the same ordered option list for every input order of a fixed option set. Starting from any such order and averaging a listwise readout over its K cyclic shifts removes the input order, but the decision still depends on the chosen cyclic class: those $K$ shifts are only one of the (K-1)! classes, and different invariant operators can select different classes. We propose IJev, which repeatedly reorders the options by the cyclic-averaged, label-prior-corrected distribution and runs another cyclic average. Every iterate is exactly input-order-invariant. When the iteration does not converge, we average the round distributions rather than return the last round. On five benchmarks and five models, IJev has flip rate zero in every cell. The default uniform average over T=20 rounds substantially improves calibration over a single cyclic average, and its accuracy is comparable. A descriptive choice of horizon and averaging rule is best or tied-best for accuracy in all 25 settings.

title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
summary: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.

title: Hierarchical Asynchronous Federated Learning over Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks
summary: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). Unlike conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, HAFL employs asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergences for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives, respectively, and formulate optimization problems to jointly determine optimal hyperparameters to minimize global training latency. Evaluations demonstrate that HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for benchmark DNNs and datasets, offering promising FL systems across remote areas with 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

title: Constraint Dependency Graph Retrieval for Compliance Detection on Long SKILL Documents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents carry out business operations under enterprise documents we refer to as SKILL documents, which take the form of standard operating procedures (SOPs) that state the conditions to verify and the actions to take before an operation proceeds. Long, densely cross-referenced SKILL documents exceed the context budget of small deployed auditors. Similarity-based retrieval then brings in irrelevant rules while omitting mandatory prerequisites, and the two-stage audit policy provides no trainable signal for the retrieval stage. We present SkillCDG, a compliance detection framework that reformulates each SKILL document as a constraint dependency graph, shifting rule retrieval from similarity-based matching to closure-based selection under the deployment's context budget. Each atomic rule is anchored to its source text span as a graph node, and mandatory prerequisite relations form the sole edge type. Policy-generated retrieval keywords activate seed rules, whose dependency closure yields a compact and conditionally complete rule context within that budget. The same graph also supports a joint optimization scheme. The retrieval stage is trained with group-relative policy optimization using a verifiable reward that combines output-format validity with downstream verdict correctness, with closure non-emptiness serving as a validity gate, while selective on-policy distillation concentrates teacher supervision on high-entropy reasoning tokens, with verdict and termination tokens always included, to improve verdict accuracy. Experiments on three enterprise datasets and two public benchmarks show that SkillCDG improves accuracy and F1 over the full-document and retrieval-based baselines.

title: Efficient Conformal Calibration for Paired Recommendation Decisions
summary: Risk control can suppress useful changes to a frozen recommendation rule. We study how to recover valid activation from the same observed fractional losses. Two specified internal calibrators can lose efficiency by compressing losses into their sum or clipping auxiliary inverse counts before averaging. We propose Averaged Conformal Risk Calibration, or ACRC, which averages before clipping. A product identity proves expected-risk validity, while pointwise bounds characterize the additional activation. For fixed populations sampled without replacement, we connect activation to signed utility under heterogeneous users and switching constraints. Near the budgets, positive population mean gain and the stated nondegeneracy conditions give positive leading-order utility increments despite sampling dependence. Across six datasets, changing only calibration improves discounted net utility by $0.010226$ over raw and $0.008337$ over RB. A separately frozen Jester confirmation gives $0.011025 \pm 0.001082$ over raw with the rule and filter fixed, using a five-seed approximate 95 percent paired interval. Against information-matched SCoRE selecting risk or reward scores, the mean utility difference is $+0.015934 \pm 0.001440$. These gains use more mean realized risk within the declared budgets. Upstream failures delimit the benefit: efficient calibration releases useful modifications when the proposals themselves have value.

title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Task-Free Federated Continual Forecasting via Two-Tier Replay under Concept Drift
comment: Peer-reviewed and accepted for presentation at the AGCS 2026 conference
summary: Federated time-series forecasting is increasingly important in applications where temporal data are distributed across privacy-sensitive clients, such as environmental monitoring, smart cities, and industrial sensing. A central limitation of current continual-learning protocols is that they usually assume predefined task boundaries, whereas deployed forecasting systems receive an uninterrupted stream and must decide autonomously when adaptation is necessary. This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting under concept drift. We introduce a drift-aware continual-learning protocol in which each client monitors prediction-window RMSE, calibrates a robust median threshold from the offline base period, and triggers adaptation only after persistent degradation. To mitigate forgetting, we propose a TwoTierReplay mechanism that separates fixed offline representative memory from online memory. The offline tier preserves long-term knowledge learned during the base phase, while the online tier captures recent distributional changes after drift. Experiments on the Beijing Multi-Site Air- Quality dataset with 12 clients, three forecasting targets, and three horizons show that TwoTierReplay achieves the best stability-plasticity score in all nine target-horizon configurations. It improves over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%. These results suggest that explicit temporal structuring of replay memory is a practical and effective mechanism for task-free federated continual forecasting.

title: What Does a Safety Label Measure? Auditing Situational-Safety Benchmarks for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Situational-safety benchmarks label each scene SAFE or UNSAFE and score a multimodal large language model (MLLM) against that label, usually by judging its free-form answer, and these scores guide deployment. We ask what such a label measures. A label score can come from the scene, the request or the benchmark's own files. We propose the Benchmark Card, seven measured fields that tell them apart, and fill it for six benchmarks. Only MSSBench chat leaks the label through its image files: image size alone reaches 82.3% accuracy, matching or beating six of seven commercial models. Elsewhere the signal outside the scene comes from design. In MOSSBench the item partition fixes the label, and on HoliSafe the request alone ranks pairs about as well as the scene. On our corrected chat split, the size rule falls to chance. We then introduce the Spot-Stop decomposition, which compares ranking with labelling on pairs of a safe and an unsafe scene. It splits the gap above a label-swap null into three parts: a threshold part, overlap between safe and unsafe scores, and order that holds only within a pair. Most of fourteen open MLLMs rank better than they label, beyond what their AUROC predicts. On chat, one shared threshold repairs a third to a half of the excess, and label-free recentering recovers it on balanced batches. Recentering on unlabelled scenes of the same situation improves ranking on VSCBench for 13 of 14 models.

title: HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.

title: Rethinking LLM Pruning via Test-Time Scaling
summary: Structured pruning reduces the size of large language models, often at the cost of lower accuracy. Whether this decline reflects diminished reasoning capacity or greater difficulty in sampling correct solutions is less clear. We examine this question across expert, FFN and layer pruning on four mathematical and coding benchmarks, comparing original and pruned models through pass@k at matched sampling budgets. Even after substantial pruning, some models match or exceed the original model's reasoning coverage despite lower pass@1, and solve problems left unsolved in the original samples. Retaining broad coverage, however, does not mean that correct solutions remain easy to obtain. Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.

title: Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models
summary: Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.

title: EMG-Hybrid: A Dual-Engine Elite Memory--Guided Adaptive Optimization Framework for High-Dimensional Feature Selection
summary: Feature selection in ultra-high-dimensional, noisy datasets remains a critical challenge due to exponential search space growth, where conventional binary metaheuristics often suffer from premature convergence. To address this, EMG-Hybrid is introduced as a novel three-level hierarchical optimization architecture designed around decoupled operational planes, feedback-driven scheduling, and isolated state refinement. At Level 1, a Dual-Engine Controller monitors population Shannon entropy and empirical fitness velocity, functioning as an architectural master-switch that dynamically routes execution between global exploration and local intensification. This control loop conditions the Level 2 active optimization plane, where an Adaptive Black Hole Gravity (ABHG) execution layer performs aggressive feature manifold pruning via a distance-decoupled penalty kernel driven by fitness similarities and Hamming metrics. To structurally isolate macro-exploration from micro-exploitation, Level 3 encapsulates an autonomous Elite Memory Archive that preserves high-fidelity sub-schemas and hosts a discrete bitwise Differential Evolution (DE) micro-refinement sandbox for resolving complex parameter epistasis. Theoretically, uniform combinatorial bounds derived via Vapnik--Chervonenkis (VC) dimension criteria demonstrate that this multi-level restriction mitigates high-dimensional overfitting. Empirical results across manifolds scaling up to $d > 100{,}000$ features, complemented by high-performance computing (HPC) profiling under lock-free atomic Compare-and-Swap (CAS) primitives, indicate strong performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines. The framework exhibits near-linear parallel speedups, sub-quadratic runtime scaling, and substantial dimensionality reduction, offering a scalable and structurally innovative paradigm for large-scale data mining.

title: CivicBench: A Benchmark and Memory Framework for Web-Based Civic Data Analytics
summary: Municipalities publish service requests, geographic boundaries, weather observations, demographic estimates, and operational guidance through independently maintained Web portals. Civic analysis must combine these sources while preserving their schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes, and interpretive limits. Tool-using language agents can perform this integration, but existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by the records used. We present CivicBench, a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years that materializes civic Web data into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation. Executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers, and refusal when the requested conclusion is not supported. We also introduce Task-State Memory (TSM), which compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints. Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences with 95\% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the ninth interval crosses zero. The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.

title: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors
summary: Low Tucker rank tensors provide compact representations of multidimensional dependencies, but standard learning pipelines can incur substantial computational and memory overhead from redundant intermediate quantities. We reduce this overhead without modifying the underlying representation objective or parameterization. Our approach combines three complementary components: (i) sequential extraction of only task-required spectral components, avoiding unnecessary full decompositions; (ii) factor-wise multilinear contractions without materializing large Kronecker operators; and (iii) compact latent-state updates without storing full ambient tensor iterates. These components preserve the algebraic operations and learning trajectories of the original algorithms while reducing their computational and memory footprints. Across five low Tucker rank tensor estimators, our implementations match the original trajectories to numerical precision (relative discrepancies of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-13}$), while reducing per-iteration runtime by up to $3.12\times$ and resident memory by up to $616\times$ ($99.8\%$) on the main order-3 benchmark at $n=100$, with memory reductions exceeding $900\times$ across the full evaluation suite. These results show that substantial computational redundancy can be eliminated from Tucker representation learning without changing the underlying model or learned representation.

title: Concept-Guided Prompting Strategies Increase Diversity in LLM-Generated Recipe Populations
summary: Novelty in solution generation supports automated discovery, but LLM outputs can remain repetitive. To address this, we propose a simple concept-guided prompting method that generates thematic concepts before responses within each of these concepts. To demonstrate, we generated 1,000 recipes for a recipe book task and compared the results against a human-authored corpus. Two naive prompting strategies were compared as baselines. Concept-guided prompting outperformed both baselines in all cases and reached semantic coverage of 47.0% versus 35.1% and 13.1% in respective prior-title and nonce prompt strategies. These findings suggest broader population exploration and diversity, but remain contained to this specific task. Further work is needed to determine the quality of solutions and generalizability.

title: ArSciKids: Arabic Curriculum-Aligned Datasets for Scientific Experiment and Multiple-Choice Question Generation in Primary Education
summary: Despite growing interest in Arabic natural language processing, curriculum-aligned educational resources remain scarce compared with English, and few public datasets for Arabic curriculum content with structured, generation-ready annotations are available, particularly for primary-school science. We introduce ArSciKids, a collection of two Arabic datasets designed for curriculum-aligned educational content generation: (1) a scientific-experiments dataset containing 999 manually curated records from official primary-school science textbooks in Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Jordan, and (2) an assessment-question dataset containing 2,167 multiple-choice questions collected from the Saudi Manhaji educational platform. The experiment records are structured with titles, objectives, tools, procedures, observations, conclusions, keywords, and grade levels, while the assessment records contain lesson references, questions, four answer options, correct answers, and explanations. Both datasets cover grades 1-6 and consist of real-life Arabic educational content rather than machine-translated or synthetically generated material. We assess the usefulness of these resources for generation by fine-tuning ten open models spanning sub-billion to several-billion parameter scales using LoRA. Models are evaluated using automatic metrics, including ROUGE and BLEU, and answer accuracy for multiple-choice generation. Moreover, we evaluate the results using a five-criterion human evaluation protocol. The results show substantial differences across model scales and tasks. ArSciKids will be publicly available, and we hope that it provides a manually curated, structured foundation for research on Arabic educational NLP, curriculum-aware generation, and low-resource language modeling.

title: Mathematical Formulation and Comparative Performance Evaluation of Machine Learning Algorithms for Maize Land Suitability Prediction
summary:
Addressing the food needs of a growing population is one of the major challenges of developing countries like Ethiopia. Various policies aimed at increasing food production have been enacted by governments and development partners. Although efforts in this regard have been made, there is still inadequate emphasis on increasing food production through the use of high technology practices. Precision agriculture using technology has been utilized to increase crop yield. Precision agriculture also relies on identifying land for a crop, which is a key factor that affects crop yield. Traditional methods of assessing land suitability for crop production are time-consuming, costly and unreliable. Against this background, the aim of this study was to assess the potential of machine learning (ML) in improving the speed and accuracy of assessing land suitability for maize, a staple crop in Ethiopia, as compared to traditional methods. The study is investigated in three areas (Burie, Shindi and Tilili) in the Amhara region. Data collection was done through the local agriculture offices and survey teams. The data were coded, scaled and balanced. Various feature extraction techniques, which included Univariate Feature Selection(UFS), Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation(RFECV) and Sequential Feature Selection(SFS), and various classifiers, which were K-nearest neighbor (KNN), gradient boosting (GB),random forest (RF) with mathematical formulations were employed. The best models were constructed through combining GBOOST and SFS and achieved an accuracy of 99.41% and 99.35% for both precision and recall. Our results showed that using machine learning is a reliable method of assessing land suitability for maize in Ethiopia.
  Keywords: Maize, Gradient boosting,Land suitability,Machine learning, Mathematical formulations

title: Learning What to Ask and What to Believe: Distilling a Variational Bayesian Agent into Language Models
summary: Interactive tasks such as eliciting a user's preferences or diagnosing a hidden mechanism require an agent to track its uncertainty over a latent state, ask informative questions and act on the answers. Language models have no explicit mechanism for this, whereas Bayesian information seeking provides one through posterior inference and expected information gain (EIG), and we ask whether it can be distilled into an 8B language model. Our teacher, a lightweight Bayesian agent with a sequential variational belief and EIG query selection, matches or approaches exact and particle references on three task families. We generate synthetic interactions with the teacher on episodes disjoint from the benchmark and fine-tune \Student{} to reproduce its queries and its belief state as a structured scratchpad. On three Multi-Turn Puzzles tasks the student raises Circuit Decoding from 0.00 to 0.93 success, lowers the normalized rank of the recommended film from 0.50 to 0.10 and cuts word guessing from 32 to 3.4 attempts, exceeding the strongest reported language models on the two comparable tasks. Exposing the belief state closes much of the gap where the decision is an implicit computation rather than a read-out of the interaction; in matched teacher contrasts, EIG supervision consistently outperforms random querying, whereas greater inference fidelity does not uniformly improve the distilled student; a 70B language-model teacher does not match the Bayesian teacher in downstream student performance, and the learned skill does not transfer to an unseen task family. Variational Bayesian information seeking can thus be amortized into a language model by transferring the belief state that drives its questions and decisions.

title: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
comment: 35 pages, 16 figures, 19 tables. Code, data, and the ConfabQA benchmark: https://github.com/vkazei/confabqa
summary: Faced with an unanswerable question, small language models can either refuse or confabulate: confidently produce a wrong answer. Can the hidden state before the first generated token provide a clue? Can we flip confabulations into refusals? I introduce ConfabQA, a 784-item benchmark whose obscure-pre-cutoff category breaks the typical correctness/knowledge-cutoff confound and map the geometry of the hidden state with linear probes, a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and direct optimization of intervention directions. On Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma 2 2B the probe separates upcoming refusals from confabulations well beyond prompt features (+7.4/+16.3 pp); on Llama 3.2 3B the ConfabQA margin is within fold-to-fold spread, but a direct refusal probe on PopQA and TriviaQA recovers +18-25 pp. On Qwen I closely inspect three candidate directions for the refusal vector: probe-recovered, Qwen-Scope SAE feature, and directly optimized. Although the three directions are pairwise 50-81 degrees apart, a push at or below the state's own norm along any of them flips most confabulations into refusal openings dominated by the "As..." family. Forcing the opener without touching the hidden state yields the same one-in-three judged-refusal rate as any push. The opposite push collapses refusals mostly into confabulations, yet leaves originally correct answers intact, so the direction gates the opening speech act rather than the knowledge behind it. Confabulations do not resolve into a concentrated feature in a dictionary or a token signature on Qwen3-1.7B. Scoring every probe on the margin over the strongest of four prompt-feature baselines extracts the hidden state's own contribution. Correctness signal is model-dependent and portable only for Llama 3.2 3B: 81% of the probe's margin over test majority survives transfer between ConfabQA, PopQA, and TriviaQA. Benchmark, judge, and code are released.

title: Character-Name Concentration in LLM Fiction: Measuring Displacement and Mitigating Repetition
summary: Character names in large language model (LLM) fiction concentrate on a handful of recurrent names such as 'Elara' and 'Elias', a measurable face of AI slop. Existing fixes either require logit access or retraining, or operate per request and cannot control concentration across a corpus. How much prompt-level strategies reduce concentration, and at what cost to name naturalness, has not been systematically measured. We present an empirical study of name-concentration control across eight strategies and introduce speculative naming, a fine-tuning-free method that adapts the draft-verify-reject paradigm of speculative decoding from tokens to names. The method requests candidate name-sets through verbalized sampling, scores them against a SlopTracker that combines a per-model fingerprint with a runtime counter, and selects through a temperature-controlled rule or its strict variant (HARD). We use 20 LLMs to generate 44,782 stories in four languages from text and visual stimuli (88,919 named characters), and measure concentration with a list-free collision metric (Slop Ratio, SR) decomposed into known and emergent components. List-based strategies do not remove slop: static banlists displace concentration to emergent names and more than halve the share of attested real names. Speculative naming removes it: the sampling scaffold alone cuts SR by 89% on average, the dynamic tracker brings the total reduction to 95%, mean collision probability falls from 7.3% to 0.4%, and known-name collisions hold at zero while naturalness stays close to baseline (42-69% attested by language) and within-story collisions drop from 4.3% to 0.2%. The strategy ranking is stable across languages, model families, and name-counting conventions. Name concentration is thus controllable at the corpus level without logit access or retraining; broader creative diversity beyond naming remains open.

title: From Policing Provenance to Designing for Evidence: Testing Four Propositions on Generative AI Against Research and Institutional Policy
summary: Generative AI has made it hard to establish whether a student produced a piece of assessed work. Building on the argument that validity matters more than cheating, this paper tests four propositions drawn from a strongly stated position: that redesign is more sustainable than detecting or banning AI; that asking students whether and how much AI they used yields low-value information; that unaided ability should be tested directly in controlled conditions; and that the same logic applies to peer review. The propositions are tested against two purposively sampled, coded corpora: 41 research and sector sources and 55 university and sector policy documents. Coding was by a single coder and the policy sample is UK-weighted, so counts describe the sample, not the sector. The propositions hold unevenly. Redesign over detection is well supported, but only as redesign plus assurance: 4 of 55 documents prohibit AI by default, though about 10 of the 55 are publisher or editorial policies that govern authors rather than student assessment; of the 23 that take a position on detection, 16 reject detectors and one requires them. Testing unaided ability is supported as one lane within a programme, not as a return to invigilation. The disclosure proposition is complicated: institutions treat disclosure as valuable, yet the limited evidence suggests many students do not complete required declarations. The peer-review extension is plausible but under-examined. The field is converging on graded permission scales and two-lane designs, and 31 of 55 documents define named categories of use. From these findings the paper builds a nine-step decision chain that extends outcome-first design logic: the role of AI is decided after the evidence an outcome requires. It also separates design moves that add temporary friction from those that provide assurance. A worked example and the full policy matrix are included.

title: XDecideBench: Evaluating Typed Decision Models and Confidence Policies Across Languages
summary: Applications use Typed Decision Models to route and moderate text in many languages, and they often act only on decisions above a confidence threshold. We introduce XDecideBench, a benchmark of nine suites in 122 languages with 88,425 texts and 153,875 typed questions. All suites share one scoring contract, and we report aligned, locally labelled and native items separately. Model rankings change from suite to suite. The model that is best in English, chosen in hindsight, loses significantly in about a quarter of the suite-language cells, and on Burmese Belebele it falls far behind the best model. Three open models fine-tuned for typed decisions beat the Qwen models they were built from in all twelve development languages. When the Qwen models are run locally, a pre-registered held-out cohort confirms that the accuracy gain is larger in the four languages with the least web text than in the six with the most. In both sets of languages, however, fine-tuning fixes a similar share of the base model's errors, so the larger gain may reflect weaker base models. A confidence threshold set on English data to allow 5% errors exceeds that error rate on XNLI, even in German and French.

title: Information-Theoretic Design of Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based activation steering is a lightweight approach for modifying the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by adding small vectors to hidden states during inference. However, designing effective steering interventions remains challenging. In this work, we develop an information-theoretic framework for analyzing SAE activations through empirical feature-firing distributions. The central object of the framework is the Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) between such firing distributions, which quantifies how far a generated or intervened state deviates from a dataset-induced target distribution. Based on an analytic divergence response for virtually shifted states, we construct steering vectors toward the target firing distribution. The same divergence can also be used to monitor deviation from another empirical distribution, such as a general valid-language distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the steering in a question-mode generation task study. We further use teacher-forced pulse experiments to show that local interventions induce structured downstream JSD responses in later layers, and apply the framework to a safety-related target--contrast response setting for feature analysis.

title: Learning by Doing: Autonomously Compiling and Curating Agent Skills from Verified Traces
summary: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $τ^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the gain is on the tasks that the teacher solved. On ALFWorld, Skills compiled from the runs of a small model give a gain similar to or larger than the gain that prior work reports for continuous fine-tuning, with no training.

title: Latent Harness: Compiling Agent Behaviors into Post-Block Activation Shifts
summary: Harness engineering and self-evolving agents improve language-model agents quickly, yet their gains live outside the model. The harness is re-sent and re-paid on every call, and the standard route to internalization is a weight update that is costly to iterate and fixed once merged. We propose compiling the harness instead. Latent Harness distills an external condition into a rank-8 activation shift. The shift is applied at the output of every decoder block of a frozen backbone, at 0.03-0.05% of parameters. The condition is either an explicit process-level behavior instruction or the behavioral contract of an agentic harness. At inference the compiled bundle carries no harness text and adds no tokens. It exposes three runtime controls for injection strength, injection phase, and shift-space mixing. Compiled behaviors recover the source-harness gain in 8 of 10 preregistered settings. Where the explicit source pays the heaviest per-call token tax, the compiled form exceeds it. The same bundles transfer zero-shot across tasks (5 of 7 pairs positive) and compose in shift space, while stacked text instructions interfere destructively. Used as a search space, they lift budget-matched harness search by 1.45 times. On three agentic benchmarks the operator aligns policy to the harness con- tract. Under matched data, capacity, and effective strength it outperforms same-capacity LoRA, which needs 11.1 times the parameters to reach the same band, and it regresses nothing where the base policy is already strong. Across 1B-to-8B models the method skeleton is invariant while gain locations move with the model-task pair, which delimits where compiled harnesses should be deployed.

title: Towards Fine-grained and Robust Detection of Human-AI Co-authorship
summary: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping how textual content is produced, complicating text provenance, and raising concerns for misinformation, plagiarism, and intellectual property. While prior work on AI-generated text detection has progressed, one-dimensional human-AI co-authorship scores lack signals directly relevant to ``AI involvement''. It remains unclear how adversarial paraphrasing distorts detection signals. In this work, we formulate a discrete-class text provenance detection framework. This framework allows an abstraction of realistic co-authorship scenarios into distinct degrees of AI involvement, differentiating the AI polishing on the surface level from the AI updating the discourse structures. This framework reveals the mechanisms of how adversarial paraphrasing blurs the decision boundaries for co-authorship detectors. To improve robustness of the detectors, we augment training data with adversarial paraphrases generated by the state-of-the-art paraphrasing attack model, exposing detectors to challenging meaning-preserving rewrites. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and generation models demonstrate that adversarial paraphrasing substantially degrades detectors trained only on benign data, while adversarial data augmentation leads to consistent robustness gains and good cross-generator transferability. Overall, our findings highlight the value of discrete-class formulation and principled data augmentation for building reliable detectors of human-AI co-authorship.

title: I-PTC: Interactive Programmatic Tool Calling for Stateful Tool-Augmented Agents
summary: Large language models are increasingly capable of writing and executing code, suggesting a natural paradigm for tool-augmented agents: expressing tool use as programs rather than isolated calls. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) captures this idea through loops, batching, abstraction, and structured computation, but existing PTC approaches are largely stateless, limiting their ability to reuse intermediate results and adapt over time. This is problematic for real-world tasks, where tool environments and problem-solving processes are inherently stateful. We therefore present I-PTC, an interactive framework that executes stateful PTC: models issue code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. To evaluate the effectiveness of I-PTC and the general PTC setting, we introduce PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style user requests whose difficulty comes from large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures. Experiments on PTC-Bench show that I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets while substantially reducing token consumption over conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline, highlighting stateful programmatic tool calling as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.

title: Accounting for Irregular State Transitions through Belief Estimation in Online Medical Consultation
summary: While online medical consultation broadens access, unprompted patient disclosures and topic shifts frequently disrupt clinician inquiry, leaving clinical states progressively revealed. We characterize these dynamics using both existing evaluation metrics and task-specific interaction metrics designed in this work. Through an empirical study across 16 medical dialogue datasets, we show that authentic online interactions exhibit substantially lower contextual continuity and higher unpredictability than offline and simulated benchmarks. We propose PRISM (Policy Reasoning with Inferred States for Medicine), a framework inspired by partially observable Markov decision processes that decouples latent state estimation from action selection to address drifting dialogue trajectories. Specifically, PRISM factorizes clinical triage into belief estimation, policy optimization, and response realization. By maintaining an evolving posterior belief over consultation states and conditioning action selection on the maximum a posteriori state, PRISM advances clinical goals while accommodating patient-initiated shifts. Extensive evaluations show that PRISM substantially outperforms frontier LLMs and clinical agents, achieving a 22.40 percentage point gain in clinical decision accuracy alongside decisive improvements in response generation, surpassing the strongest baseline by 5.51 points in BERTScore_F1. Furthermore, ablation studies show that providing oracle consultation states consistently boosts response quality across all evaluated baselines by guiding their action reasoning, yielding average gains of 5.58 points in BERTScore_F1.

title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
